title: CUDA Toolkit 13.4 Adds Windows on Arm Support and Greater Control over Shared GPUs | NVIDIA Technical Blog
gist: CUDA Toolkit 13.4 opens developer access to Windows on Arm and a preview compute-capability target (SM_107) for NVIDIA's next-generation Rubin GPU architecture months ahead of its general-availability release, while also modernizing GPU multi-tenancy controls (MPS V3), adding a new NVLink fabric transport API, and shipping a Blackwell-specific CUB scan kernel that reaches 92% memory-bandwidth utilization — together signaling NVIDIA's platform roadmap is already actively courting Rubin-era software portability and denser shared-GPU utilization ahead of hardware launch.

themes.theme: Rubin architecture preview and platform expansion

insights.claim: CUDA Toolkit 13.4 adds preview functional support for the NVIDIA Rubin GPU architecture (compute capability 107 / SM_107), letting developers begin porting applications before CUDA support for Rubin reaches general availability in a future toolkit release.
insights.speaker: Jonathan Bentz
insights.so_what: NVIDIA is giving the developer ecosystem multi-month lead time to port software to Rubin before hardware GA — a recurring NVIDIA pattern that shortens the real-world time-to-productivity of each new GPU generation and is worth tracking as a leading indicator of Rubin's actual launch timing.
insights.quote: CUDA Toolkit 13.4 adds functional support for the NVIDIA Rubin architecture (compute capability 107) as a preview, enabling developers to begin porting applications before CUDA support for Rubin reaches general availability in a future release of the CUDA Toolkit.
insights.locator: Developer access to NVIDIA Rubin as a preview

insights.claim: NVIDIA explicitly frames Rubin as 'the next-generation GPU architecture powering the era of agentic AI,' tying the hardware roadmap directly to agentic-AI workloads as the stated design driver rather than generic AI training/inference.
insights.speaker: Jonathan Bentz
insights.so_what: NVIDIA's own marketing/positioning language ties its next silicon generation to agentic AI specifically — useful signal for how NVIDIA expects to frame Rubin's differentiated value proposition to enterprise/hyperscaler buyers versus prior 'generative AI' framing for Blackwell.
insights.quote: Rubin is the next-generation GPU architecture powering the era of agentic AI.
insights.locator: Developer access to NVIDIA Rubin as a preview

insights.claim: CUDA Toolkit 13.4 extends CUDA application development to Windows on Arm for the first time, having previously supported Arm only through Linux; Core math libraries (cuBLAS etc.) gain Windows on Arm support specifically for the 'N1X Laptop ecosystem.'
insights.speaker: Jonathan Bentz
insights.so_what: Signals NVIDIA actively building out CUDA compatibility for Arm-based Windows laptops (the 'N1X' ecosystem reference implies a specific upcoming Arm PC platform) — relevant to NVIDIA's push into the Windows-on-Arm client/PC GPU market alongside Qualcomm and Microsoft's Arm PC initiatives.
insights.quote: Core math libraries in CUDA Toolkit 13.4 now have functional support for the Rubin GPU architecture and Windows on Arm support for the N1X Laptop ecosystem.

insights.claim: On NVIDIA's coherent-memory platforms (Grace Hopper, Grace Blackwell, and Vera Rubin), the CUDA driver now defaults to Coherent Driver-based Memory Management (CDMM) instead of NUMA mode, a node-wide setting change that requires a driver reload or reboot and should be evaluated before upgrading.
insights.speaker: Jonathan Bentz
insights.so_what: A default behavior change on production coherent-memory clusters (Grace Hopper/Blackwell/Vera Rubin) is an operational risk item for any infrastructure team running large GPU fleets — teams need to explicitly evaluate and potentially pin NUMA mode before upgrading to avoid unplanned performance/behavior shifts.
insights.quote: On NVIDIA coherent platforms like NVIDIA Grace Hopper, NVIDIA Grace Blackwell, and NVIDIA Vera Rubin, the driver now defaults to Coherent Driver-based Memory Management (CDMM) instead of NUMA.
insights.locator: Coherent Driver-based Memory Management default for coherent platforms

themes.theme: Multi-tenant GPU control and shared-infrastructure economics

insights.claim: Multi-Process Service V3 (MPS V3) introduces a modernized control layer for shared GPUs with a scriptable CLI, named server instances, namespaces, TOML configuration, streaming-multiprocessor (SM) partition controls, and cgroup-integrated GPU memory limits, enabling precise programmatic GPU partitioning for containerized environments.
insights.speaker: Jonathan Bentz
insights.so_what: Better native GPU partitioning/isolation tooling directly serves the GPU-cloud and neocloud business model (renting fractional GPU capacity to many tenants) — this is infrastructure investors in GPU-as-a-service providers should track as it lowers the engineering cost of safe multi-tenant GPU sharing, a key unit-economics lever for those providers.
insights.quote: This release ensures that MPS integrates into containerized environments, maximizing hardware utilization while maintaining strict resource isolation for every process.

insights.claim: CUDA 13.4 exposes programmatic access to 'locality domains' — GPU regions containing specific streaming multiprocessors and device memory — letting applications co-locate compute with the memory it accesses on GPUs that have more than one locality domain, improving performance.
insights.speaker: Jonathan Bentz
insights.so_what: Indicates NVIDIA's newest large GPUs increasingly have internal NUMA-like memory locality structure requiring explicit software management — a sign of growing chip-level complexity that raises the bar for low-level CUDA optimization work and favors sophisticated software teams/vendors who can exploit it.
insights.quote: A locality domain is a portion of a GPU that contains streaming multiprocessors (SMs) and device memory. ... Co-locating computation near the memory it accesses can improve performance on devices with more than one locality domain.

themes.theme: New NVLink fabric transport for communication-library developers

insights.claim: CUDA Compute Fabric Transport (CFT) is a new transport-centric API that lets communication-library developers move data across NVLink fabric using named logical endpoints (endpoint ID plus offset) with asynchronous put/get/reduction operations issued directly from the GPU, instead of mapping every remote GPU allocation into a process's virtual address space.
insights.speaker: Jonathan Bentz
insights.so_what: Reduces virtual-address pressure in very large multi-GPU systems and supports unicast/multicast patterns with error detection/retry/reroute — foundational plumbing that benefits scale-out GPU cluster communication libraries (NCCL, NVSHMEM) and thus the largest AI training clusters; CFT itself is a low-level Driver API aimed at library developers, not application developers directly.
insights.quote: This approach reduces virtual-address pressure in large multi-GPU systems, supports unicast and multicast communication patterns, and reports completion and error status so applications can detect, retry, or reroute failed fabric transfers.

insights.claim: A new warp-specialized cub::DeviceScan implementation for Blackwell GPUs, using the Tensor Memory Accelerator (TMA) to overlap memory movement and computation, reaches up to 92% memory-bandwidth utilization versus roughly 50% in the previous implementation, across tested data types.
insights.speaker: Jonathan Bentz
insights.so_what: A ~1.8x jump in memory-bandwidth utilization for a core primitive (device-wide scan) used across many GPU algorithms is a concrete, measurable software-only performance gain on existing Blackwell silicon — relevant to any workload bottlenecked on scan-heavy operations getting a free speedup purely from a toolkit upgrade, no hardware change needed.
insights.quote: the new cub::DeviceScan::Sum implementation reaches up to 92% memory-bandwidth utilization (from up to around 50% in a previous implementation) across the tested data types.
insights.locator: Faster device-wide scans on NVIDIA Blackwell GPUs

insights.claim: On Blackwell data-center GPUs, cuBLASLt now dynamically schedules Grouped GEMM computations across streaming multiprocessors to minimize load imbalance in common mixture-of-experts (MoE) workloads, improving performance particularly for Grouped GEMM calls with many groups (e.g., 32) and when Grouped GEMM runs concurrently with other device kernels.
insights.speaker: Jonathan Bentz
insights.so_what: Direct software-level performance improvement for MoE inference/training specifically on Blackwell — as MoE architectures (used by many frontier models) proliferate, this kind of kernel-level optimization compounds NVIDIA's hardware advantage with matching software gains, widening the practical performance gap versus competitors relying on generic kernels.
insights.quote: On Blackwell data center GPUs, cuBLASLt dynamically schedules Grouped GEMM computations across streaming multiprocessors (SMs) to minimize load imbalances in common MoE workloads.

insights.claim: CUDA 13.4 ships cuda.core 1.1.0 with .pyi type stubs for every public API, explicitly described as giving both IDEs and 'coding agent access to type information, function signatures, return types, and more' — an explicit design accommodation for AI coding agents, not just human developers.
insights.speaker: Jonathan Bentz
insights.so_what: A small but telling signal that NVIDIA is now designing developer-tool APIs with AI coding agents as a first-class consumer alongside human developers — worth watching as a broader industry pattern in developer-tooling investment (agent-readable APIs becoming a stated design goal).
insights.quote: cuda.core 1.1 provides .pyi type stubs for every public API, giving IDEs autocompletion and coding agent access to type information, function signatures, return types, and more.

insights.claim: NVIDIA Nsight AI adds a hosted CUDA MCP Server that connects supported AI coding agents to current CUDA documentation and code examples, plus an open-source, self-hostable 'Nsight Copilot Blueprint' for teams preferring to run their own CUDA AI backend.
insights.speaker: Jonathan Bentz
insights.so_what: NVIDIA is building its own Model Context Protocol (MCP) server product to plug CUDA-specific knowledge into AI coding agents, plus offering an on-prem/self-hosted version — a direct entry into the AI developer-tooling/agent-infrastructure space that investors tracking MCP ecosystem adoption should note.
insights.quote: The NVIDIA-hosted CUDA MCP Server connects supported AI coding agents to current CUDA documentation and code examples, while the open-source Nsight Copilot Blueprint provides a self-hosted CUDA AI backend for teams that prefer to deploy and operate it in their own environment.

insights.claim: CUDA SDK installers no longer bundle the NVIDIA driver as of Toolkit 13.4; developers must install the nvidia-open driver or cuda-toolkit packages separately via their package manager, decoupling driver and toolkit release/update cycles.
insights.speaker: Jonathan Bentz
insights.so_what: A packaging/operations change that affects every CUDA deployment pipeline (CI, containers, fleet management) — infra teams need to update install/upgrade automation to explicitly manage driver versioning separately from the toolkit going forward.
insights.quote: CUDA SDK installers no longer bundle the NVIDIA driver. Install the appropriate nvidia-open driver or cuda-toolkit packages separately, using your preferred package manager.
insights.locator: Decoupling the CUDA driver and the CUDA toolkit
